asl.hook: The fluttering finger is like the puff of air that leaves your mouth when you say "who."
steps: Make an L handshape with your dominant hand: index finger and thumb out.
Touch the tip of your thumb to your chin.
Bend your index finger twice (a small flutter at the knuckles), keeping the thumb on your chin.
When asking a question, furrow your eyebrows; in a statement ("he didn't tell me who"), keep them neutral.
asl.tip: Lifeprint also accepts an X hand wiggling in front of the chin without touching, but recommends the thumb-on-chin version. An older version circling the mouth is outdated.

fact.text: The Arctic tern has the longest migration of any animal: every year it flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back. One tracked tern covered nearly 60,000 miles (about 96,000 km) in a year, more than twice the circumference of the Earth.

lead.headline: Two Italians killed in drone attack in Kuwait; Iran denies role and calls incident 'suspicious'
more: A source cited by Reuters said the two Italians were technicians working for the German defense company Rheinmetall. Kuwait said its army had detected drones in its airspace and that an air defense system was targeted.

Araghchi said Iran was offering cooperation over the incident, without giving details. President Trump said the United States had victory at hand and was giving Tehran a chance to negotiate a deal to prevent further loss of life.

The attack comes amid a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, stalled U.S.-Iran talks and an escalating exchange between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition, with the Houthis claiming strikes on Riyadh, Jeddah, Jazan and the Ras Tanura refinery earlier this week.
lead.summary: Two Italian nationals were killed in Kuwait on Thursday by falling debris as forces tried to intercept drones over what Kuwait's Defense Ministry called a vital site, in an attack Kuwait blamed on Iran. Four other people were injured. Iran's armed forces denied carrying out any military operations in the region, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the incident suspicious, describing it as a pre-cooked recipe for war. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the attacks unacceptable and urged more pressure on Tehran.

briefs.text: The federal government is authorizing further withdrawals from its mandatory jet fuel reserves as supply problems abroad leave stocks at Swiss airports running low; Zurich and Geneva airports had already drawn on the stockpile in recent weeks.

The franc strengthened again as investors sought safety after new US tariff threats; on Wednesday the euro fell below 91 centimes, its lowest level since May, after trading near 95 centimes at the start of October.
From January 1, 2027, pregnant women will pay no deductible or co-payment for care during the whole pregnancy; the exemption currently starts only in the 13th week.

stories.headline: Switzerland reports first AI-driven cyberattacks on critical infrastructure
more: Florian Schuetz, the office's director, told public broadcaster SRF that critical infrastructure in at least two sectors was affected and that private companies were also targeted. It remains unclear who was behind the attacks.

The AI programs hunt for weak passwords and software flaws far faster than human hackers and switch methods when defenses respond. The office said the number of freely available AI agents online has nearly doubled since October.
Authorities urged operators to cut the number of systems reachable from the internet, install updates quickly, tighten access rights and use multi-factor authentication.
stories.summary: The Federal Office for Cyber Security has confirmed five cases of attacks carried out with autonomous AI agents, three of them aimed at critical infrastructure. Two of those three succeeded, though the office's director said they caused no major disruptions.

stories.headline: Federal Council proposes single flat-rate deduction for work expenses
more: The deduction would not depend on workplace or income and would apply to full-time and part-time workers alike. The government said the change would make filing easier for taxpayers and checks simpler for cantonal tax offices. No start date has been set.
stories.summary: The Swiss government wants to replace several separate work-related tax deductions with one flat-rate allowance that requires no receipts. The allowance would cover all professional costs, including meals away from home.

briefs.text: The trial of Ilona W., a 57-year-old German-Ukrainian businesswoman accused of spying for Russia on military aid to Ukraine, drone test sites and the arms industry, was due to open in Berlin on Thursday but was delayed because of her health.
North Rhine-Westphalia's state parliament banned face veils in schools, with exceptions for medical masks, and gave principals power to suspend students for up to four weeks over violence or threats.

BSW parliamentary leaders in eastern Germany unanimously backed working with the AfD where majorities allow, a stance party founders called misguided ahead of the BSW federal convention in Dresden on Friday.

Berlin had Germany's highest car theft rate in 2025, with 3,082 comprehensively insured cars stolen, about ten times the national average, though thefts in the city fell 20 percent, insurers' association GDV said.

stories.headline: Two Iraqis arrested over alleged plot against synagogue in Cologne
more: Prosecutors link the suspects to the pro-Iranian group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia (HAYI) and say the two founded a separate cell in Germany in late 2025. Arrest warrants were issued on November 18.

According to the investigation, unknown persons scouted synagogues in Cologne and the other city on two consecutive nights in late March. The alleged plan was not carried out, and it is not known why.
An investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe will decide whether the men stay in pretrial detention.
stories.summary: Federal police arrested two Iraqi men, aged 31 and 34, in Heidelberg and Cologne on Thursday on suspicion of membership in a terrorist group. Federal prosecutors say the group planned attacks on a synagogue in Cologne and one in another European city.

stories.headline: Police arrest three more teenagers suspected of belonging to far-right 'Terror 18'
more: The group is accused of planning an arson attack on a refugee shelter. Police foiled a planned arson attack on a shelter in Winsen, south of Hamburg, in October.
Three other suspected teenage members were arrested in October and remain in custody.
stories.summary: Police arrested three boys in several towns in northern Germany on Wednesday on suspicion of membership in the far-right group 'Terror 18', federal prosecutors said. Media reports say two of them are 14 and one is 15.

stories.headline: Bundestag set to pass record 2027 budget today
more: Opposition leaders attacked the plan this week: AfD parliamentary leader Tino Chrupalla called it pure debt, and Left Party leader Heidi Reichinnek called it pale and cold. Merz will miss the vote to attend an EU summit in Brussels.
stories.summary: The Bundestag is scheduled to approve the 2027 federal budget on Friday after four days of final debate. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called the largest budget in German history justifiable while signaling future spending cuts.

briefs.text: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar pledged to ratify the Istanbul Convention on violence against women, alongside measures including stronger restraining orders, a new offense for misuse of intimate images and prescription-free emergency contraception.

Nagoya University researchers developed a light-activated antibody therapy that killed the main gum-disease bacterium while sparing helpful mouth bacteria and reduced bone loss in mice; it has not yet been tested in people.

stories.headline: China's mangroves more than double, and bird species nearly triple
more: China lost nearly 70 percent of its mangroves between 1950 and 1990. The study found the number of globally threatened bird species recorded in the restored habitats rose from 11 to 21.
Worldwide, Global Mangrove Watch data show a small net gain of 477 square kilometers of mangroves between 1985 and 2025.
stories.summary: China's mangrove cover more than doubled between 1998 and 2020 after decades of loss, according to a study in The Innovation. Over the same period, the number of bird species recorded in the country's mangrove areas rose from 148 to 397.

briefs.text: The Nordic electricity system price reached 3.19 kronor per kilowatt hour on Thursday, the highest since December 2022, due to weak winds and a brief shutdown of Finland's Olkiluoto 3 reactor; relief is expected as low-pressure systems arrive.

Foreign Trade Minister Benjamin Dousa said a reported US plan for 15 percent tariffs on EU goods would put the two sides back to square one, and named counter-tariffs and export curbs as possible EU responses.
Overnight stays by foreign visitors in Sweden are up 11 percent so far this year, against 2 percent for domestic guests, industry group Visita said.

stories.headline: Centre Party leadership moves to back Kristersson as prime minister
more: The proposed government of the Moderates, Christian Democrats, Liberals and Centre Party would lack a majority of its own. The Centre Party says there will be no formal cooperation with the Sweden Democrats, who have said they would tolerate such a government without joining it.

The party's confidence council is expected to meet on Sunday to decide, broadcaster SVT reported. Not all Centre lawmakers are certain to follow the line. Monday's vote at 1 p.m. is the third attempt to elect a prime minister; if a fourth fails before Christmas, Sweden must hold an early election.
stories.summary: Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist said Thursday that her party's leadership wants to vote for Moderate leader Ulf Kristersson in Monday's prime minister vote and join a four-party centre-right government. She said the decision had majority support but was not unanimous.

briefs.text: Trump will tour TSMC's chip plant in Phoenix on Dec. 4 to mark an expansion the White House says will support more than 10,000 direct jobs.
Puerto Rico's Supreme Court voted 5-4 to end the government's contract with grid operator Luma Energy, with a one-year transition.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving storm leaves nearly 900,000 without power and floods East Coast
more: Pennsylvania had more than 200,000 customers without power, Virginia more than 150,000 and Missouri more than 100,000, according to PowerOutage.us. More than 2,000 U.S. flights were delayed and more than 420 canceled, FlightAware reported.

New York City got about 1.5 to 2 inches of rain, with up to 3 inches in places, and LaGuardia Airport recorded a 56 mph gust. Rescuers pulled drivers from flooded cars in New York City and Avalon, New Jersey; no deaths were reported.
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was moved to Saturday because of wind. In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers were asked to conserve water because of power disruptions.
stories.summary: A powerful storm swept the East Coast and Midwest on Thanksgiving, knocking out power to nearly 900,000 customers by Thursday evening and flooding coastal areas from North Carolina to New Jersey. New Jersey declared a statewide state of emergency, and parts of New York did the same.

stories.headline: Trump calls revised GDP figures a 'purposeful error' and demands investigation
more: The Bureau of Economic Analysis revises its estimates on a set schedule, and the department did not immediately comment, with the government largely closed for Thanksgiving. The same agency reported that the PCE price index, a key inflation gauge, rose at a 3.8% annual pace in October.
Trump has questioned unfavorable data before: in August 2025 he fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a weak jobs report.
stories.summary: President Trump demanded an investigation of the Commerce Department after it revised third-quarter economic growth up to a 4.3% annual rate from an earlier 3.4%. He suggested the stronger number had been held back until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which Democrats won.

stories.headline: Judge declines long-term ban on taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads
more: The DNC sued in October over at least 11 ads, paid for at least partly through a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract, some of which promoted the president and his tax cuts. A judge in New York also declined a long-term ban.
The Justice Department argued there was no ongoing harm because public funds were no longer being used for the ads. The DNC said it would keep fighting.

In a separate ruling, the same judge blocked the FCC from pursuing early license renewal reviews of ABC's eight owned TV stations while the network's lawsuit proceeds, finding ABC likely to show the review was retaliatory.
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan declined to extend a temporary ban on government ads that the Democratic National Committee says amount to taxpayer-funded propaganda, noting the midterm elections have passed. She said the DNC was nonetheless likely to succeed on its claim that using public money for the ads was illegal.

briefs.text: Israeli strikes killed at least eight people in Gaza, including a senior Education Ministry official Israel called a Hamas figure, medics said.
At least 31 people died when a fuel tanker overturned and exploded on a ring road in Giza, Egypt's Health Ministry said.
Flooding at an illegal gold mine in Indonesia's West Java killed at least 13 workers, with 13 more missing.
French film star Gerard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy warns Russia is preparing a new massive strike on Ukraine's power grid
more: Ukraine's General Staff said it damaged five Russian aircraft, three MiG-31s and two Su-34s, at Savasleyka airbase east of Moscow; Russia did not immediately comment. Moscow-installed officials said a Ukrainian drone strike killed five people in occupied Zaporizhzhia.

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said peace talks had reached a deadlock over territory. NATO says Black Sea incidents involving drones, mines and ships have jumped from fewer than 50 last year to roughly 400 to 500 in 2026.
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said intelligence shows Moscow is completing preparations for another large attack on energy infrastructure as winter nears. Russia fired ballistic missiles and 113 drones overnight, hitting 20 locations, and crews were restoring power in six regions.

stories.headline: Kim vows to expand nuclear arsenal and widen deployment of tactical weapons
more: State media photos showed what appeared to be uranium-enrichment centrifuges. Kim accused Washington of encouraging allies to seek nuclear-powered submarines.
Pyongyang did not respond publicly to President Trump's offer to meet Kim during his trip to the APEC summit in China last week.
stories.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un toured two nuclear materials factories and pledged to expand his nuclear forces in quality and quantity, state media said Thursday. He called deploying low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains crucial and urgent.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola cases pass 12,000 as fighting disrupts response
more: About a dozen people, including two WHO staff, were evacuated to Bunia after three days trapped by crossfire in a hospital in Akwe. Cases have been reported in eight of Congo's 26 provinces since the outbreak was declared in May.

In Kenya, the High Court ruled the government violated the constitution by allowing a U.S.-backed Ebola quarantine facility at Laikipia airbase without disclosure or public input, and ordered work there halted.
stories.summary: Confirmed Ebola infections in the Democratic Republic of Congo have reached at least 12,021, with 5,904 deaths, according to government data. Clashes between the army and CRP fighters in Ituri province have forced response workers out of affected areas.

fact.text: The Advent wreath is usually credited to Johann Hinrich Wichern, a Lutheran pastor who made one in 1839 at the Rauhes Haus mission school he founded in Hamburg. His version had 24 small red candles, lit on weekdays and Saturdays, and four large white ones for the Sundays, which is where today's four-candle wreath comes from.

german.literal: to stand in front of the door
german.meaning: to be just around the corner, to be coming up very soon (an event or season)
german.note: Used for holidays, seasons and deadlines: Weihnachten steht vor der Tür, der Winter steht vor der Tür. Literally a person can also stand at the door, so context makes the meaning clear.

onThisDay.text: The United States held its first national day of thanksgiving under the Constitution on Thursday, November 26, 1789. President George Washington had proclaimed it that fall after Congress asked him to recommend a day of public thanksgiving. Abraham Lincoln later modeled his 1863 proclamation on Washington's, and that year's Thanksgiving also fell on November 26, as it does again today.
onThisDay.title: First national Thanksgiving

lead.headline: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including the EU, Switzerland and China
more: The investigations followed the Supreme Court's February ruling that struck down the administration's earlier tariffs imposed under an emergency powers law, which led to refunds.

Other proposed rates include 18 percent for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, up to 25 percent for India without a deal (17 percent with one) and up to 35 percent for Vietnam without a deal. Mexico and Norway remain under investigation but face no new tariffs for now.

Capital Economics said the move was less alarming than it looks because the new duties would largely replace existing ones rather than stack on top. A small-business coalition said the tariffs would raise prices during the holiday season.
lead.summary: The Trump administration proposed new tariffs on China, the European Union and 12 other economies, including Switzerland, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and India, under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Proposed rates include 15 percent on top of normal duties for the EU, Japan and Switzerland, and up to an additional 20 percent for most Chinese goods, which would bring China's total to about 45 percent. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said many partners use industrial strategies that tilt trade in their favor and erode U.S. manufacturing. No effective date has been set, and comments are due Jan. 5 before public hearings begin Jan. 25.

briefs.text: The European Commission fined the three biggest fragrance makers 471.9 million euros for a cartel that ran from 2019 to 2023 and targeted Unilever. Geneva-based Givaudan was fined 252.4 million euros and Firmenich 137.7 million; Britain's competition authority added 85 million pounds in fines.

Russian financial assets frozen in Switzerland rose to 8.5 billion francs as of July 1, up from 7.45 billion in March 2025, the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs said, citing new seizures, adopted EU sanctions and higher gold prices.

An SRF investigation of court rulings since 2020 found 169 women in Switzerland survived attempted femicides; about 40% of the attacks involved strangulation. The annual "16 days against violence against women" campaign began Wednesday with a focus on online abuse.

stories.headline: US threatens new tariffs of up to 15% on Swiss goods over 'overcapacity'
more: The finding rests on Section 301 of the US Trade Act. The new duties would come on top of most-favored-nation rates and existing tariffs, with some goods exempt; the US already applies 12.5% tariffs to Switzerland, citing forced-labor concerns.

Bern said it expects any measures to respect a November 2025 declaration of intent between the two countries that aimed to cap US tariffs at 15%, down from a previously announced 39%. The Swiss government had not received official notice by Wednesday afternoon, and the tariffs are not expected to take effect before January.

The business federation economiesuisse sharply criticized the move, saying Switzerland has no export subsidy programs and does not add to global excess capacity. China, the EU, Japan, South Korea, India and Vietnam face the same threat.
stories.summary: The US Trade Representative said Wednesday that Switzerland is among 14 economies whose industrial policies unfairly burden American commerce, opening the way to new tariffs of up to 15% on Swiss imports. Washington cited Swiss currency policy, support for the pharmaceutical industry and cheaper electricity for steelmakers. The Swiss economics ministry rejected the accusations and said it would study the US report before deciding how to respond.

stories.headline: European Parliament approves Swiss-EU treaty package by wide margin
more: The package updates existing accords on air and land transport, free movement of people, mutual recognition of product testing and farm trade, and sets terms for Swiss participation in EU programs. Lawmakers voted in Strasbourg without debate.

An accompanying resolution on EU-Swiss relations passed 554 to 22. It points to possible further cooperation, including a financial services agreement and Swiss participation in the EU civil protection mechanism, which could start in 2028.
stories.summary: The European Parliament on Wednesday approved the package of agreements updating relations between Switzerland and the EU, 584 to 13 with 60 abstentions. The deal covers Swiss access to parts of the single market and adds new accords on electricity, health and food safety. Ratification now moves to the Swiss parliament, and a Swiss popular vote is not expected before 2028.

stories.headline: North Korea expels head of Swiss office in Pyongyang weeks after it reopened
more: The Songdowon International Children's Camp is accused of helping Russia indoctrinate Ukrainian children taken from occupied areas; the EU and Britain also sanction it. Switzerland adopted the related EU sanctions package in early November, freezing the camp's assets abroad and barring its leaders from entry.

Kim Yo-jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong-un, had threatened on Tuesday to close the mission. Switzerland had said it would keep talking to Pyongyang. The office reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing; an earlier Swiss cooperation office closed in 2020 during the pandemic.
stories.summary: North Korea declared Sylvain Astier, head of Switzerland's diplomatic office in Pyongyang, persona non grata and gave him 48 hours to leave. Pyongyang also demanded that the office close, calling Swiss sanctions on a children's camp near Wonsan a hostile act. Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis had opened the office on Oct. 19.

stories.headline: Swiss government sends parliament a softer alternative to corporate responsibility initiative
more: Due diligence duties would cover firms with more than 5,000 full-time jobs and global turnover above 1.5 billion francs. Liability would depend on proven fault, with the burden of proof on the person harmed, following similar EU rules.

Penalties were reduced from the draft put out for consultation in April, and reporting rules would follow the EU's recently relaxed requirements, roughly halving the number of companies that must file sustainability reports to about 110. The Federal Audit Oversight Authority would monitor compliance.
stories.summary: The Federal Council on Wednesday sent parliament its counter-proposal to the Corporate Responsibility Initiative, which would require companies to respect human rights and the environment abroad. Justice Minister Beat Jans said the draft law would apply due diligence rules to about 30 to 60 of the largest Swiss companies. The government rejected the initiative's call to make firms liable for the acts of business partners.

briefs.text: Veruschka, born Vera Countess von Lehndorff and known as Germany's first supermodel, died in Berlin at 87, her family said. Her father was executed in 1944 for his role in the plot to kill Hitler; she later worked with Richard Avedon, Irving Penn and Helmut Newton.

Chancellor Merz pledged better protection against femicides after the Bundestag held a minute of silence for victims. Federal police figures show 342 women and girls were killed in Germany in 2025, 209 of them by partners or relatives.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he was shocked that President Trump intervened in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, saying governments in democracies should not meddle in companies.
The Greens plan to propose a 10 million euro federal fund in December to help save village pubs and other community meeting places, citing similar programs in Spain and Ireland.
The German Weather Service said beech trees changed color about nine days later and dropped their leaves about 10 days later than the 1992-2025 average this year, possibly a record late leaf fall.

stories.headline: Merz defends record debt-funded budget ahead of Friday Bundestag vote
more: The plan foresees about 560 billion euros in core spending, roughly 36 billion more than this year, and nearly 140 billion euros for defense, the most since the end of the Cold War. The Federal Court of Audit has warned the country is on a path toward a debt trap.

AfD parliamentary leader Tino Chrupalla called the borrowing a story of superlatives and accused Merz of political failure. The Left and the Greens also attacked the debt and the financing of a planned electricity tax cut, which critics say is secured for only one year.
Coalition budget experts say tougher savings targets for 2028 are to be set early next year. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul criticized the spending cuts imposed on his ministry.
stories.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz defended the 2027 federal budget in the Bundestag's general debate on Wednesday, arguing that new borrowing of about 210 billion euros is needed for defense and long-neglected infrastructure. In an unusually defensive speech, he conceded that the coalition's budget process did not deserve a beauty prize. The Bundestag holds its final vote on Friday.

stories.headline: Berlin Left Party expels lawmaker as talks on Left-led city government enter final phase
more: Group leader Tobias Schulze said relations with Emde had become irreconcilable after she withdrew her signature from a party statement against antisemitism and joined a protest against the party. Emde called the controversy a smear campaign and plans to stay on as an independent.

The Left placed first in Berlin's September election and hopes to make lawyer and housing activist Elif Eralp the city's first far-left mayor. Working groups in the coalition talks are due to report by the end of this week.
stories.summary: The Left Party's group in Berlin's state parliament expelled lawmaker Vanessa Emde of Neukolln, who had been accused of antisemitism over her criticism of Israel. Her removal clears one obstacle in coalition talks with the Social Democrats and Greens, which both had pushed for it. The three parties aim to present a coalition agreement by early January.

stories.headline: German business morale holds at highest level since 2023
more: The survey comes as Berlin prepares a record budget funded by heavy borrowing for defense and infrastructure; the Bundestag votes on it Friday.
stories.summary: The Ifo Institute's business climate index rose to 90.6 points in November, slightly better than analysts expected and matching October's level, the highest since May 2023. Ifo president Clemens Fuest said companies were more satisfied with current business and had raised their expectations.

briefs.text: Smooth-coated otters, a vulnerable species, are now seen regularly along Kuala Lumpur's Klang River, once rated Class 5, Malaysia's worst category for pollution. Years of cleanup, including hundreds of garbage traps and solar-powered waste interceptors, have lifted it to Class 3, and advocates want it clean enough for swimming next.

New York City recorded 359 overdose deaths from April to June 2026, its lowest three-month total since 2019 and 58% below the record 859 in late 2022, according to city Health Department figures announced Nov. 13.

Finland's white-tailed eagles, once rare across Europe, have been growing about 9% a year in both the Baltic Sea and Lapland populations, a University of Turku study in Oikos finds, crediting legal protection, cleaner environments and high adult survival.

stories.headline: Cancer vaccine extends survival in late-stage leukemia trial
more: The REGAL trial randomized 126 patients who had reached a second or later remission and could not have a stem cell transplant. The vaccine targets WT1, a protein found in the cancer cells of more than 95% of AML patients. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate injection-site reactions, with no new safety signals.

The results are topline data from the company and have not yet been peer reviewed. SELLAS plans to talk with the FDA and aims to file for approval in the first half of 2027. The vaccine was invented at MSK, which licensed it to SELLAS in 2014 and has a financial interest in it.
stories.summary: An off-the-shelf peptide vaccine, galinpepimut-S, helped patients with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia live longer in a pivotal phase 3 trial, developer SELLAS Life Sciences and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center said on Nov. 17. Median overall survival was 24 months with the vaccine versus 14.7 months with the best available treatment, a 41% reduction in the risk of death.

briefs.text: New polls show the Moderates gaining amid the government standoff: Demoskop puts them at 25.8%, up 6 points since the election, while the Liberals fell to 3.2%, below the 4% threshold for parliament. Indikator put the Centre Party at 4.8%.

The Migration Agency paused so-called teen deportations of some young adults who were ordered out when they turned 18, pending a temporary law expected in autumn 2027. Agency chief Maria Mindhammar called the pause an exception.
The Financial Supervisory Authority warned that rapid AI development, high asset valuations and geopolitical tension raise the risk of global market turmoil that could spill over into Sweden.

stories.headline: Centre Party splits over Kristersson ahead of Monday's prime minister vote
more: Kristersson proposes a four-party government of the Moderates, Christian Democrats, Liberals and Centre Party, which Sweden Democrat leader Jimmie Akesson says he will tolerate.

The party's women's and youth wings oppose the shift, as does its Stockholm district, while the Skane and Vasternorrland districts back talks with the right. About 35 local and regional politicians signed an op-ed urging the party to rule out any government reliant on the Sweden Democrats.
Several party sources quoted by the TT news agency suggested the Centre Party could abstain, letting Kristersson through, and then go into opposition.
stories.summary: Sweden's Centre Party is under growing internal pressure as parliament prepares to vote Monday at 1 p.m. on giving Moderate leader Ulf Kristersson another term as prime minister. Leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist reopened talks with the centre-right bloc after centre-left negotiations collapsed, but any Kristersson government would depend on the Sweden Democrats, whom the party had vowed to keep from influence. An online meeting of party lawmakers and local officials on Tuesday ended without decisions.

briefs.text: The Army detonated the nation's stockpile of unstable lead azide explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday; Gov. Kim Reynolds said early feedback from experts was that the blast was successful.
A federal jury in New York convicted Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets and of bank fraud but acquitted it of racketeering conspiracy; the company said it will appeal.
Six members of a Florida family died when their small plane crashed into the Gulf off the Mississippi coast on Tuesday while returning from a fishing trip; the FAA and NTSB are investigating.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving storm postpones Macy's parade for the first time as East Coast braces for wind and flooding
more: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill declared a statewide state of emergency from 6 p.m. Wednesday, warning of damaging winds, heavy rain, coastal flooding and possibly long power outages; Cape May, Atlantic and Ocean counties face the greatest flood risk. Record coastal flooding is forecast for Delaware Bay.

Boston and Philadelphia are expected to get a cold, steady rain, though most big cities should avoid the highest totals. Up to 9 inches of snow was possible in parts of Illinois and Missouri, including the St. Louis area.

The parade had never been postponed for weather; it was suspended from 1942 to 1944 during World War II. About 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday, and significant delays were possible at Northeast airports on Thursday.
stories.summary: A powerful coastal storm moving up the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day led Macy's to postpone its 100th parade in New York to Saturday, citing safety concerns about the storm and the giant balloons. Forecasters warned of wind gusts up to 70 mph from South Carolina to Massachusetts, heavy rain and coastal flooding, with more than 44 million people under alerts on Wednesday.

stories.headline: Scrutiny grows over White House role in Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO
more: According to CBS News, the administration assured the board that Huang was not a target of a Justice Department investigation. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department has no evidence of wrongdoing by Huang or Nvidia but did not clearly say whether it is investigating them.

California's attorney general has subpoenaed Nvidia over whether advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether investors were misled. The Justice and Commerce departments are investigating Megaspeed, and Nvidia's board says its own outside review will continue.
Huang faces closed-door questioning by three House committees on Dec. 1 and a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on Dec. 3. Democrats have demanded information about the administration's role.
stories.summary: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid reports about his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China, which it denies. President Trump said he "convinced" the board to bring Huang back, and CBS News reported that he and Vice President JD Vance spent the weekend talking with Huang and board members.

stories.headline: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves the U.S. for Spain, ending long deportation fight
more: On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis closed his civil case and lifted her injunctions after confirming he had left. DHS said he will never be allowed back into the country; his lawyer said a path to permanent residency exists but would need a State Department waiver.
Human smuggling charges against him were dismissed in May by a Tennessee judge who found the prosecution vindictive. The Justice Department has appealed, with arguments set for February.
stories.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man wrongly deported to El Salvador in 2025 and later returned, flew to Madrid on Tuesday with his U.S.-citizen wife and his lawyer. The Department of Homeland Security said he left under a removal order and paid for his own flight, while his attorney said the government failed in its effort to send him to Liberia.

stories.headline: Army moves to resume helicopter training flights near Reagan National Airport
more: Sen. Maria Cantwell urged the FAA to block the flights until new safety measures and a full risk assessment are in place. A House-Senate deal in principle would require aircraft to carry systems that show nearby traffic with visual and audible alerts, and Sen. Ted Cruz wants it passed before January.
stories.summary: The Army plans to resume helicopter training flights near Washington's Reagan National Airport, where an Army helicopter collided with an American Airlines jet in January 2025, killing 67 people. NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said the flights could restart as early as Dec. 1, but the FAA says it has received no formal request and must approve any restart.

briefs.text: An Israeli strike on a home in Gaza's Shati refugee camp killed Muhammad Abu al-Awf, head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, along with his wife and two daughters, Gaza's Interior Ministry said.
Rescuers in Indonesia's West Java are searching for 26 people trapped in a flooded, unlicensed gold mine about 60 km south of Jakarta after a nearby river overflowed, police said.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became Pakistan's first astronaut, launching on China's Shenzhou-24 and docking with the Tiangong station, the first non-Chinese national to reach it.
Bangladesh's garment industry wage board raised the monthly minimum wage 36 percent, to 17,500 taka (about $136), after weeks of protests; higher pay arrives in January.
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for lifting the U.S. fuel blockade on Cuba, saying it harms Cubans, and pledged $2 million for the island's vaccination program and medical equipment.

stories.headline: Houthis threaten Saudi ports after coalition strikes Hodeidah; Iran reports another tanker hit by mine
more: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship carrying liquefied natural gas hit a naval mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday evening, a claim that could not be independently verified. No casualties were reported.

Iran's army said vessels that pass without coordinating with Iranian forces face greater risks. Tehran has said it will not restore normal shipping until the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and ends the war on all fronts, and through Qatari mediators has offered to reopen the strait within 48 hours of those conditions being met.

Hodeidah is the main entry point for food and other supplies into Houthi-held northern Yemen. Qatar and Pakistan, which are mediating between Iran and the U.S., condemned the attack on the Riyadh tower.
stories.summary: Yemen's Houthis threatened Saudi Red Sea ports including Jeddah after the Saudi-led coalition struck the Houthi-held port of Hodeidah, and urged port workers and shipping companies to leave. Saudi air defenses shot down at least seven drones over the Eastern Province on Wednesday, the coalition said, a day after a Houthi drone hit Riyadh's tallest tower and injured at least 11 people, according to Saudi authorities.

stories.headline: Leaked Russian records point to at least 490,000 soldiers killed in Ukraine war
more: The dataset holds more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026. By the analysis, war deaths made up 65 percent of all deaths among Russians aged 18 to 24 in 2025.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said only Russia's Defense Ministry can disclose casualty figures. In May, the head of Britain's GCHQ put Russian military deaths at about 500,000.
stories.summary: Hacked Russian government death records analyzed by the BBC and the independent Russian outlet Mediazona indicate that at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022. The data was obtained by the pro-Ukraine hacker groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow.

stories.headline: Eisenkot signs first coalition partner in bid to replace Netanyahu
more: Likud and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies hold 53 of 120 seats, against 48 for Eisenkot's party and partners. Talks with Likud on a possible unity government continue, and the left-wing Democrats suspended talks with Eisenkot over them. asl.meaning: Like, to like something (I like it!)
steps: Use your dominant hand and start a bit out from your chest.
Point your middle finger and thumb back toward your chest, without touching it.
Move the hand forward, away from your chest.
As it moves, bring the finger and thumb together so the sign ends in an 8 handshape.
Check the Lifeprint photos for the exact start and end positions.
asl.tip: Lifeprint notes LIKE means enjoying something, not similar (that is SAME). DON'T-LIKE reverses the orientation to make the negative. Practice: YOU LIKE COFFEE? (Do you like coffee?)

fact.text: Flamingos are not born pink: the chicks hatch a dull gray and only take on color as they eat. Their pink comes from beta carotene, an orange-red pigment in the algae, larvae and brine shrimp they feed on, which their bodies break down and deposit in their feathers and skin.

lead.headline: Iran says tankers hit mines in Hormuz and rules out US talks until its conditions are met
more: The conditions reported so far include lifting the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, easing sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over. Iran's foreign ministry called the blockade tantamount to military aggression. A maritime information center that recorded 114 U.S.-assisted passages through the strait from Nov. 19 to 21 said the mine claims were unconfirmed.

On Monday the Treasury Department sanctioned 22 entities and eight people it says form an Iranian shadow banking network spanning Iran, Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey. The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was behind cyberattacks on as many as 50 commercial ships.

Qatar's prime minister met Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance in Washington on Monday to try to revive U.S.-Iran talks, saying the region cannot bear a renewed escalation. President Trump said on Sunday that military strikes on Iran could resume after the New Year.
lead.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said three oil tankers suffered explosions and fires after striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, two of them while under U.S. air escort; the claim has not been independently confirmed. Iran's army chief ordered the navy to tighten control of the strait day by day until Washington meets Tehran's demands, and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said there would be no negotiations before Iran's seven conditions are implemented. Washington, meanwhile, widened sanctions on Iran's financial network.

briefs.text: Lawmakers are considering mandatory psychological tests for anyone buying a firearm, a debate fueled by a fatal shooting at a rave in Aarau in August. The gun lobby Pro Tell calls blanket checks disproportionate.
Two parliamentary committees approved letting foreign airlines fly the long-abandoned Geneva-Lugano route; parliament takes up the issue in its December session.
UBS economists expect Swiss rents to rise by about 5 percent by early 2028, linked to an expected shift in Swiss National Bank interest rate policy.

Rebuilding the Pontifical Swiss Guard barracks at the Vatican will cost 70 million francs, up from 45 million; 61 million has been raised, a public campaign starts in December and work is due to run from spring 2027 to about the end of 2029.
Forecasters expect colder weather this week with a good chance of snow flurries in the lowlands, and wintry roads especially in eastern and central Switzerland.

stories.headline: Swiss House committee backs 90 percent capital rule for UBS foreign units
more: The committee rejected the Federal Council's 100 percent proposal by 17 votes to 7 and a 75 percent option by 12 to 8 with five abstentions. A sizable minority wanted to set the ratio at 80 percent.
stories.summary: A committee of the National Council voted 13 to 12 to require UBS to back its foreign subsidiaries with equity capital covering 90 percent of their value. The decision matches the Senate's position from September and is softer than the government's proposed 100 percent. The full House still has to vote.

stories.headline: Switzerland says it will keep talking to North Korea despite threat to its Pyongyang office
more: The EU accuses the camp of taking part in a program that moves Ukrainian children from occupied territories to North Korea in coordination with Russia. Switzerland adopted the EU's 21st sanctions package against Russia, which covers the issue, in early November.

The Pyongyang office reopened in October after closing during the Covid-19 pandemic and reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing. Bern said the reopening had nothing to do with its sanctions policy. Switzerland and North Korea have had diplomatic relations since 1974.
stories.summary: The Swiss foreign ministry said it remains committed to dialogue with North Korea after Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, threatened to close the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang. The threat appeared linked to Swiss sanctions on a North Korean children's holiday camp. The ministry said no official contact or formal demands had yet been received.

stories.headline: Switzerland taps more emergency jet fuel reserves as airport stocks run low
more: Zurich Airport receives most of its fuel by rail from Germany and Geneva through a pipeline from France, and both routes have limited capacity. Train cancellations and problems at European refineries have slowed deliveries, and tanks at Swiss airports are very low.
The released fuel must be sold on the Swiss market. The economics ministry said the measure will be lifted once supply improves for good.
stories.summary: Switzerland will allow further withdrawals from its compulsory aviation fuel reserves from November 30 to head off shortages at its airports. About 18 percent of the stockpiles were released between mid-October and the end of November, close to the 20 percent the supply office can approve on its own. Officials expect demand to rise in December.

briefs.text: Pay talks between IG Metall and metal and electrical industry employers resume on Wednesday in Mannheim, after a wave of 24-hour strikes at plants including Mercedes, BMW, Porsche and Audi. The union wants 5 percent more pay over 12 months; employers have offered a one-off payment in 2027 and a 1.3 percent raise from July 2028.

Investment in German tech start-ups is set to nearly triple this year to 8.1 billion euros from 2.9 billion, according to a study by the German Start-up Association and the Joachim Herz Foundation, driven by large rounds for robotics and defense-tech firms.
President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said he was disappointed that the COP31 climate conference ended without a final agreement, saying during a visit to Ivory Coast that the world must act together.

stories.headline: German report says Russia could put a nuclear-armed satellite in orbit within weeks
more: The satellite, reportedly called Sputnik-S, is said to have been assembled and stored near Moscow for several years. A nuclear blast in orbit could knock out many satellites, and its electromagnetic pulse could disrupt communications and power grids on the ground.

Russia's embassy in Berlin said it had no information on the matter, called the claims part of a propaganda campaign and said its space activities are peaceful. The reporting relies on anonymous sources and has not been independently verified.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which Russia has joined, bans nuclear weapons in orbit. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, speaking alongside Merz in Berlin on Monday, said the alliance would defend all its territory, including its assets in space.
stories.summary: An investigation by public broadcasters WDR and NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung, citing intelligence sources, says Russia could launch a satellite carrying a nuclear warhead by the end of the year. An assessment from early November reportedly put a possible launch within 60 days. Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm the reports but said he was deeply concerned.

stories.headline: Bundestag opens final week of debate on record 560.9 billion euro budget
more: The plan includes 123 billion euros of net new borrowing in the core budget, and more than 200 billion euros in total once debt-financed special funds are counted. Investment is put at 126.7 billion euros for infrastructure, hospitals, schools and the armed forces.

A late compromise adds a one-year cut in electricity tax worth about 5 billion euros and grid-fee subsidies of about 5.5 billion euros a year from 2027 to 2029. Opposition parties have focused on the scale of the borrowing.
After Friday's vote the budget goes to the Bundesrat and the federal president, and is due to take effect on January 1.
stories.summary: Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil opened four days of Bundestag debate on the federal budget for 2027, which at 560.9 billion euros would be the largest on record. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is due to answer the opposition AfD in Wednesday morning's general debate on government policy. A final vote is set for Friday.

stories.headline: Five members of one family found dead in Kehl apartment, carbon monoxide suspected
more: The dead also included the children's 46-year-old father and their 74-year-old grandmother. Police were called on Monday after several children failed to show up for school and no one answered the door.

Prosecutors in Offenburg are investigating and said it is still unclear whether a technical fault or a crime caused the deaths. Other flats in the building were checked, and police said there was no further danger.
stories.summary: Five members of a family, including three children aged 10 to 14, were found dead in an apartment in Kehl, a town on the Rhine across from Strasbourg. Firefighters believe carbon monoxide leaked in the flat. Two other children survived with serious injuries.

briefs.text: The World Health Organization has issued its first guidelines for diagnosing and managing type 1 diabetes in adults, written for all settings including low-resource and humanitarian ones. About 9.5 million people lived with type 1 diabetes in 2025, and WHO aims for all of them to have affordable insulin and glucose self-monitoring by 2030.

Decades of water-saving upgrades have made the U.S. Northeast and Midwest far more drought-resilient, a CUNY study in Environmental Research Letters finds: peak summer water stress in a repeat of the 1960s drought would be 5.6 times lower in the Northeast and 2.8 times lower in the Midwest than with 1960s-era infrastructure, mostly thanks to more efficient water use.

stories.headline: Arctic Alaska walrus haul-out protected for good
more: Walrus began hauling out on the Point Lay islands in 2007 as summer sea ice, their usual resting platform, became unreliable. About 250,000 Pacific walrus migrate each year between Alaska and Russia. The deal, which took 10 years, also protects 20 miles of Kasegaluk Lagoon, described as one of the largest undiminished coastal lagoon systems in the world.

The land trust holds the easement and plans more monitoring to limit disturbance as shipping and tourism grow, since human intrusion has set off deadly stampedes among resting walrus in the past. Funding came from a North American Wetlands Conservation Act grant and several private foundations.
stories.summary: The Conservation Fund and the Interior Alaska Land Trust, working with Alaska Native groups, have placed 47,473 acres of barrier islands and adjoining mainland off Point Lay, Alaska, under a permanent conservation easement. The islands are where more than 200,000 female and juvenile Pacific walrus have come ashore to rest every year since 2007.

stories.headline: Speaker schedules Monday vote on Kristersson as Sweden's prime minister
more: The Centre Party has not agreed to back a Kristersson government and says its refusal to depend on the far-right Sweden Democrats still stands. Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson told the Speaker she currently has no path to forming a government but that her door remains open.

This would be the third prime ministerial vote since the September election, and Sweden has gone more than 70 days without a permanent government. If four votes fail, a snap election must be held within three months; Norlén said Swedes should know before Christmas whether there will be a new government or a new election.
stories.summary: Speaker Andreas Norlén nominated Moderate leader Ulf Kristersson for prime minister and set a parliamentary vote for Monday, November 30, at 1 p.m. The move follows the Centre Party's decision to resume talks with the Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals after centre-left negotiations with the Left Party collapsed. Kristersson is elected unless 175 or more lawmakers vote against him.

President Trump was scheduled to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Rudy Giuliani, 82, his former personal lawyer, in an Oval Office ceremony on Tuesday.
Pennsylvania reported its ninth measles death this year, in Centre County; its outbreak of more than 1,600 cases is the largest in the country.

stories.headline: Unsealed warrant shows search of Rep. Omar's home sought records dating to 1980
more: Homeland Security Investigations agents carried out the search on Oct. 12 under a warrant signed Oct. 9 by a magistrate judge, at the request of U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office. Investigators could take documents, photos, drives, computers and phones used by Omar. Most of the 169 released pages are redacted.

The records show the judge questioned probable cause for at least two offenses and required that Omar be allowed to flag protected legislative material before it was searched. WCCO reported, citing sources, that several immigration issues are under investigation. Omar's office has said she did nothing wrong and called the search an abuse of power.
stories.summary: A federal court released documents on the October search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home, showing investigators were authorized to seize records tied to alleged violations from 1980 to the present. No charges have been filed, and the specific statutes in the warrant are redacted.

stories.headline: Justice Department pulls litigators from other divisions to fight ICE detention suits
more: Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote that U.S. attorneys' offices are overwhelmed by the petitions and called many of them frivolous. About 10,000 were filed since October; before Trump's second term such petitions numbered in the hundreds per year.
The memo does not say how many lawyers will be reassigned. The rise in cases follows record numbers of people in ICE detention and narrower options for release on bond.
stories.summary: A Justice Department memo directs attorneys from the antitrust, civil, civil rights and environment divisions, among others, to help defend the government against lawsuits from immigration detainees. More than 97,000 detainees have filed habeas corpus petitions challenging their detention since January 2025.

stories.headline: 21 states sue HUD over rule ending housing aid for mixed-status families
more: Mixed-status families now receive prorated aid. The rule also requires landlords and housing authorities to report tenants who fail verification to the Department of Homeland Security. A HUD audit identified about 20,000 such households nationwide, and California's attorney general said 7,000 households in his state would be affected.
HUD says the rule closes loopholes and will redirect up to $218 million to eligible Americans on waiting lists.
stories.summary: Twenty-one states and Pennsylvania's governor sued the Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule that would deny federal housing assistance to any household that includes a member without eligible immigration status. The rule takes effect Dec. 14.

stories.headline: Shein to pay $100 million to settle FTC deception claims
more: The FTC said Shein had only five customer service representatives for U.S. phone calls while shipping about 1 million packages a day to the country. The proposed order requires adequate customer service and bars misleading delivery claims. Shein said the deal is not an admission of liability and that it disagrees with parts of the FTC's account.
stories.summary: Online retailer Shein agreed to pay $100 million to settle Federal Trade Commission allegations that it broke shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews and made misleading claims about its suppliers' labor standards and cotton sourcing. The money will go toward refunds for customers.

briefs.text: Masked gunmen took an unknown number of hostages at a supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia, after a failed armored-truck robbery, police said; the city's airport briefly suspended operations.
Mexico will put alleged cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, on trial at home despite a U.S. extradition request, the attorney general said.
The World Food Programme told the UN Security Council that disruption at the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb and the Black Sea puts food aid for 7.3 million people at risk.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged countries to agree within a year on a global framework for managing AI risks, backed by independent oversight.

stories.headline: Sheikh Hasina says she will return to Bangladesh from exile on Dec. 16
more: Hasina has asked to be flown home from Delhi on the national airline and says she will fight the verdict, though the judiciary says she missed the appeal deadline. She is expected to be arrested on arrival. The UN estimates up to 1,400 people were killed in the 2024 uprising that ended her 15-year rule.
stories.summary: Former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia over the deadly 2024 crackdown on protesters, plans to return from India on Dec. 16, her spokesman said. The government says she is a convicted fugitive and has requested her extradition.

stories.headline: Malaysia to send more than 6,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar
more: About 1,500 people are to go by navy ship on Dec. 6 and 7, and 5,303 more will be flown back at Myanmar's expense. Rights groups have criticized an earlier return in September, and Malaysia had sought clarification about reports that returnees were held in military detention. The ICJ ruling requires that returns be safe, voluntary and dignified.
stories.summary: Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the country will return more than 6,500 Rohingya refugees to Myanmar in December, saying it can no longer afford to host them. The announcement came five days after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar's forces committed genocide against the Rohingya.

stories.headline: Australia moves to fine tech giants up to 5% of global revenue for online harm
more: Targeted harms include child sexual abuse material, fake nude images, self-harm promotion and terrorism, and individuals could sue platforms. Users 16 and older could switch off algorithm-driven feeds. Tech firms oppose the bill, saying it gives officials too much discretion over what counts as harmful.
stories.summary: Australia's government unveiled a digital duty of care law requiring platforms such as Google and Meta to proactively find and remove harmful content, with penalties of up to 5% of worldwide revenue. The bill is expected to pass Parliament this week with Greens support.

lead.headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, and Trump says he urged the board
more: The reversal surprised many: on the previous week's earnings call, Jones had said the company did not plan to bring Huang back. Colette Kress had served as interim CEO. Trump said the government had no evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang, citing Attorney General Todd Blanche, and said Nvidia should continue its internal review of export-control compliance.

Lawmakers from both parties said the questions remain. Huang is scheduled for a transcribed interview with the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China committees on December 1, and the Senate Banking Committee says he will testify on December 3. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called the reinstatement indefensible, while Republican senators John Cornyn, John Curtis, Kevin Cramer and Pete Ricketts questioned the board's reasoning.

Also on Monday, the Commerce Department added Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is accused of moving Nvidia AI chips to China and denies it, to its trade blacklist, meaning companies need a federal license to sell it advanced U.S. technology.
lead.summary: Nvidia's board on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, about 11 days after he resigned over an affair with a former executive of a Singapore data center firm whom U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China, which Beijing denies. Board chair Harvey Jones said Huang was the right person to lead the company and that, after input from senior U.S. government officials, the board concluded his return posed no national security risk. President Trump praised the decision and told CNBC he had spoken directly with the board, saying he convinced it to rehire Huang. Nvidia shares jumped more than 30 percent, helping lift Wall Street after a steep sell-off on Friday.

Home and outpatient care reached a record in 2025, with hours of care up 15.3 percent to 29.6 million, according to the Federal Statistical Office. Hospital outpatient visits rose 3.9 percent.

A new Federal Statistical Office study found Switzerland has one of Europe's highest rates of female employment but ranks among the lowest at turning it into equal pay, citing wage gaps and widespread part-time work.
Zurich has the world's most expensive cappuccino at a median 5.90 francs, ahead of Copenhagen, Paris and Geneva, according to the 2026 Cappuccino Index, which put the global median at 3.50 francs.

stories.headline: Greens nominate Geneva's Delphine Klopfenstein Broggini to challenge SVP ticket
more: The party had said in October it would not contest the SVP seat. Klopfenstein Broggini won the internal nomination in the sixth round of voting, ahead of Leonore Porchet and Sophie Michaud Gigon, and said she was running for a diverse Switzerland, with climate protection, social justice and gender equality as priorities.

Greens caucus chair Greta Gysin called the SVP nominations a provocation, and party president Lisa Mazzone said the Greens would not be blackmailed by the SVP. The Greens had already said they would not invite Aeschi and Graber to hearings, citing a 2024 scuffle between the two and security staff at the Federal Palace.
Parliament elects Parmelin's successor on December 9.
stories.summary: The Green Party on Monday nominated Geneva National Council member Delphine Klopfenstein Broggini for the Federal Council seat being vacated by Guy Parmelin, mounting a challenge to the Swiss People's Party's two official candidates, Thomas Aeschi and Michael Graber. The Greens said the all-male, all-German-speaking SVP ticket ignores women and French-speaking Switzerland.

stories.headline: Swiss machinery and metals orders jump 13 percent as recovery broadens
more: Capacity utilization edged up to 82.1 percent, still below the long-term average of 85.6 percent. Swissmem said the recovery follows three years of crisis and is gaining strength and breadth, led by energy and data center infrastructure suppliers, while tool and textile machinery makers remain under heavy pressure.

The association warned that the upturn remains vulnerable, citing the risk of reduced access to the EU market if Switzerland is treated as a third country under the EU's planned Industrial Accelerator Act, and continuing uncertainty over tariffs with the United States.
stories.summary: Orders in Switzerland's mechanical engineering, electrical and metalworking industry rose 13.1 percent year on year in the third quarter, according to the industry association Swissmem. Sales grew far more slowly, by 1.8 percent in the quarter and 2.3 percent over the first nine months.

briefs.text: A fire at a hospital in Berlin's Lichtenberg district on Sunday evening forced the evacuation of the whole building and injured 15 people, one of them critically, according to the fire department. Police are investigating the cause.

Berlin's CDU asked the state parliament to add an article to the city's constitution committing the state to fight antisemitism and protect Jewish life. The Left, Greens and SPD, now in coalition talks, favor a broader text but lack the two-thirds majority needed on their own.
Germany ranked fourth in the 2026 EF English Proficiency Index for non-native speakers, behind Sweden, Austria and Denmark, with a score four points lower than last year.

stories.headline: IG Metall widens 24-hour strikes to Mercedes, BMW and shipyards in north
more: The union says 151,000 workers joined Friday's nationwide walkout, which hit Audi's main Ingolstadt plant and three BMW plants in Bavaria. Further strikes are expected in Berlin and in Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland and Thuringia.

IG Metall is seeking a 5 percent raise over one year for 3.7 million metal and electrical workers. Employers have offered a one-time payment of 1 percent of annual pay in July 2027 and a 1.3 percent raise from July 2028, which the union says would leave workers worse off after inflation.
stories.summary: The IG Metall union called more than 23,000 workers at 19 sites in northern Germany out on a 24-hour warning strike starting Sunday night, after three rounds of pay talks failed. Production at Mercedes-Benz plants in Hamburg and Bremen stopped, and workers at BMW, Siemens Gamesa in Cuxhaven and the Meyer Werft shipyard in Papenburg were also called out.

stories.headline: Opposition attacks fuel price cap draft that exempts motorway stations
more: The Left Party's Janine Wissler accused Reiche of designing the cap to be as ineffective as possible. According to Handelsblatt, the draft went to an internal government vote on Friday evening.

The CDU-SPD coalition agreed on a price cap in September. Reiche's first version, criticized especially by the SPD, would only have applied if German fuel prices rose five percentage points more than the EU average for three straight weeks, something that has not happened even since the Iran war drove prices up.
stories.summary: Economy Minister Katherina Reiche's new draft law for a fuel price cap would exempt petrol stations on motorways, drawing sharp criticism from the opposition. Green Party leader Felix Banaszak said it would be hard to design a more absurd cap and called for a windfall tax on crisis profits instead.

briefs.text: A coalition led by Wetlands International, UNEP and FAO launched a Peatland Breakthrough at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, with Germany, Peru and Uganda as champion countries; peat soils cover about 3 percent of Earth's land but store more carbon than all the world's forests combined.

University of Pennsylvania researchers reported in Scientific Reports that a chewing gum made from lablab beans, which contain an antiviral protein, cut HPV levels by up to 93 percent in saliva samples from head and neck cancer patients in lab tests; trials in people have not yet been done.

stories.headline: Ghana becomes first African country to earn TREES forest credits
more: ART's TREES standard measures emission reductions across whole countries or large jurisdictions rather than single projects, which is meant to make the results harder to game by shifting logging elsewhere. ART did not name a buyer or a price in its announcement; Euronews, in a roundup of encouraging news from the COP31 climate talks, put the credits' value at about 40 million euros.
stories.summary: Ghana has been issued 6.57 million TREES credits for cutting deforestation and forest degradation, the first country in Africa to receive them, the Architecture for REDD+ Transactions (ART) said on November 12. The credits recognize results from Ghana's national-scale REDD+ program across about 2.5 million hectares.

briefs.text: About 1,500 patients of a dental clinic in Vaxjo are being offered tests for HIV and hepatitis B and C after a machine that cleans instruments skipped key disinfection steps. Region Kronoberg said it cannot rule out that this caused an HIV infection but called the risk very small.
The Swedish krona has fallen nearly 10 percent against the U.S. dollar this year, the weakest performance among G10 currencies.
The obesity drug Wegovy will soon be sold in tablet form in Sweden; no price has been set, but it is expected to cost a few thousand kronor a month.
Linn Svahn won her second straight race at the cross-country season opener in Bruksvallarna, edging Moa Ilar and Ebba Andersson in the 10-kilometer freestyle.

stories.headline: Centre Party reopens talks with right-wing bloc as Speaker meets party leaders
more: The offer from the Social Democrats, Centre and Greens would have given the Left Party state secretaries, a budget unit at the finance ministry and a seat in an inner circle of party leaders, but no cabinet posts. Left Party deputy leader Ida Gabrielsson rejected it within minutes, saying the party must have ministers.

Speaker Andreas Norlen meets each party's leader individually on Tuesday, starting with the Social Democrats at 9:30 a.m., and plans a news conference no earlier than 4:30 p.m. Parliament has already rejected two candidates for prime minister; a fourth failed vote would force an extra election.
stories.summary: Sweden's Centre Party will resume government talks with the Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals after the Left Party rejected an offer meant to make Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson prime minister, party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist said, according to SVT. She said further major concessions to bring the Left Party to the table were not an option.

briefs.text: Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a California Democrat, will resign next week after the House Ethics Committee found substantial evidence of sexual misconduct involving a staffer. Gomez disputes the findings.

Stocks surged Monday on Huang's return to Nvidia: the Dow rose more than 1,400 points and the Nasdaq more than 6 percent, a rebound after Friday's sell-off pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.
FIFA announced that the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will co-host the 2031 Women's World Cup, the first with four hosts and 48 teams.

stories.headline: Appeals court clears Army to detonate unstable explosives at Iowa plant
more: The Army says the material has been recrystallizing and could explode on its own, and federal officials told the court the work had to happen by Tuesday, before temperatures drop below freezing. Two environmental groups had sued to block the detonation, challenging an emergency EPA permit, and the court had paused the work last week.
Some residents worry that lead dust could spread across Iowa and into Illinois, while others say they want the job done quickly.
stories.summary: A federal appeals court ruled Monday that the Army may detonate 68 barrels of lead azide, a bomb-making material, at the World War II-era ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, PBS News reported. Earlier in the day, President Trump said he had told the military to hold off until the 8th Circuit agreed and said the operation should also depend on Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand.

stories.headline: Storms on both coasts threaten Thanksgiving travel
more: Pacific storms are expected to bring heavy rain and mountain snow to the West Coast, while a Gulf storm could bring rain, damaging winds and snow to parts of the East. Florida, already flooded after nearly a week of rain, expects more.
stories.summary: More than 3,700 U.S. flights were delayed Monday, with a ground stop at Chicago's O'Hare and lingering effects from a Delta system failure on Sunday. Delta says its operations have resumed.

stories.headline: Democrats set 12 presidential primary debates starting in June
more: Candidates must sign a pledge to publicly denounce super PAC and dark money spending on their behalf, and campaigns may not enter joint fundraising agreements with party committees during the primary. The DNC acknowledged it cannot ban outside spending. Dates, media partners and qualifying thresholds will be announced later.
stories.summary: The Democratic National Committee announced 12 debates for the 2028 nomination race, five in 2027 and seven in 2028, beginning in June 2027. Stages will be capped at 20 candidates, with crowded debates split over two nights by random draw.

briefs.text: A nationwide strike against government austerity plans shut down air traffic control at Belgium's airports on Monday, cancelling most flights, as Prime Minister Bart De Wever negotiates a budget meant to save about 10 billion euros.
Indonesian police removed 24 body bags from a candy factory in Serang regency that burned Saturday; DNA identification could take weeks, and the company said 29 workers were missing.

The death toll from a Russian strike on an apartment building north of Kyiv rose to at least 11, and Russian drones killed at least three people at a medical clinic in Zaporizhzhia, PBS News reported.
Severe drought hit more than half of Afghanistan's provinces in the past year; the UN says 22 million people need aid and 3.7 million children face acute malnutrition.

stories.headline: Iran vows to counter US blockade as Washington adds sanctions
more: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said early Tuesday that three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz; the claim could not be independently confirmed. Qatar's prime minister told Al Jazeera the region cannot withstand another escalation between the US and Iran.

The US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports in July after a June understanding collapsed. Baghaei said Hormuz could be made secure quickly if Washington met its commitments, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the shadow banking system Iran's last financial lifeline.
stories.summary: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday that Tehran would use all available means to counter what he called US military aggression, describing the naval blockade and sanctions as an act of war under the UN Charter. The US Treasury the same day sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and individuals it says form Iran's shadow banking network.

stories.headline: Unknown substance forces evacuation of 12,000 at Manchester concert
more: Greater Manchester Police declared a major incident and said they were working to establish what the substance was and how it was released. Some concertgoers initially believed it was tear gas, and the venue was decontaminated as a precaution.
stories.summary: More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live arena on Sunday night after an unidentified substance sickened people at a Don Toliver concert. More than 80 people were assessed or treated, some for eye and breathing problems, and one was taken to hospital.

stories.headline: Fighting near Ebola hospital traps health workers in eastern Congo
more: Congo's outbreak, its largest and deadliest, had caused 5,678 deaths among 11,613 cases as of November 17, according to the WHO, which says transmission remains high nationally despite slight declines in some areas. Fighting with armed groups, including the M23 rebels, has hampered deliveries to remote areas.
stories.summary: WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus appealed for peace after heavy fighting near a hospital in Ituri province forced health workers and aid staff to shelter in a maternity ward for more than 24 hours. He said the clashes put patients and staff at grave risk and disrupted the Ebola response.
